## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.50316.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.50316.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

One of the most important open problems in theoretical ecology and movement ecology in particular is whether or not observed Lévy walk movement patterns (and similar behavior) are caused by intrinsic pattern generators implemented as neuronal networks. The alternative possibility is that such movement patterns are an emergent side-effect of how animals interact with the environment. The former explanation suggests that Lévy walks etc. are adaptive, whereas the latter explanation suggests that the behavior is not evolved. This experimental paper gives what is close to a definitive answer to this longstanding question.

The experiment has been custom designed, the data carefully processed, and the analysis has been undertaken with the required high standards (for example, the authors have taken care to distinguish power laws from truncated power laws). There are several technical results that, together, paint a picture that is as surprising as it is significant. When the experimenters artificially impair brain processing of sensory information, the resulting movement paths resemble Lévy walks, supporting the idea that there is an evolved neurophysiological mechanism that generates paths resembling Lévy walks.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Optimal searching behaviour generated intrinsically by the central pattern generator for locomotion" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Ronald Calabrese as the Senior and Reviewing Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: William S Ryu (Reviewer #1); Adam J Calhoun (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

There are some concerns and needs for clarifications requiring revision. The full reviewer comments are provided and should be fully addressed, but as a guide to the revision, we emphasize a few points brought out in these reviews.

1) Both reviewer #1 (main concerns – request to check if the statistics change over time (e.g. dependent on satiety?)) and #2 (point 4 – is there any adaptation to the turn rate?) overlap and indicate the need for serious consideration by the authors of stationarity in the data.

2) The additional concerns of reviewer #2 can be characterized as two question each requiring a careful response:

a) Is a random walk model (RWM) appropriate for fly larva foraging?

For RWM, the assumption is that reorientation events are independent and that the "steps" do not have some non-trivial correlations (e.g. curvature with direction of turn, etc.). We ask the authors to show additional statistics about turns and steps in support of a RWM. In addition, inspection of the tracks in the figures makes it look like sometimes larvae are either on a curvy track or turning a lot. Our guess is that this is real, and we think some small figure emphasizing that would be not too difficult to produce. For instance, if the authors simply show that slightly different thresholds in the tracking still results in truncated power laws we would be fine with the analysis. Our main concern would simply be that all these power laws are simply a result of the particular tracking.

b) How sensitive are the results to the segmentation parameters?

The authors are looking at 1D of the 2D data set so they aren't identifying "turns" directly and so can't directly do a sensitivity test for "turn angle." Essentially, they are identifying step lengths which statistically reproduce the same exponent of the power law distribution. We ask for a better description of the segmentation pipeline for step lengths in the main text, to help clarify to readers that the analysis does not identify turns directly, since we feel this might be overlooked by some readers. Moreover, we require some comment on how sensitive these results are regarding any parameters used in this pipeline, including image processing, filtering, data exclusion (xmin), and fitting.

Reviewer #1:

This is nice work.

Stochasticity is a fundamental element of animal behavior and in the context of search is universal across a wide range of species. Recent measurements of animal movements has shown that these probabilistic movement patterns approach a Lévy distribution. Leveraging the neurogenetic power of the fly model, this work addresses important questions. How do animals generate these non-trivial distribution? How are these random number generators implemented biologically? Are they generated through sensory information, sensory processing, higher order computation (extrinsically) or through a mechanism at a lower level (intrinsically)?

I believe technically the experiments are sound and that the data analysis uses appropriate and modern statistical tests required for determining the distribution parameters. I especially appreciate the inclusion of the order of magnitude of the data range, and the transparency of the testing details shown in the supplementary files.

The authors are careful to show important controls and experimentally the tracking experiment looks also to be carefully controlled for environmental inhomogeneities. However there are two parameters that I would like the authors to comment on. In C. elegans it has been shown that searching behavior changes scale over time, slowly increasing with a tau measured in tens of minutes. Are the fly search patterns constant in time over the 1 hour experiment? Does this differ between the BL/SOG blocked conditions? Also, it is assumed in C. elegans that the change in time is due to a change in satiety levels. At the beginning of the experiment the worm is well fed and so when searching on an agar surface with no food, it looks local with a short time/length scale, but as it gets hungry it extends the searching scale. While the blocked BL/SOG condition was shown to be within a range of normal feeding (Figure 2), I wonder if there might be still be a systematic nutritional or a satiety difference that is occurring. These comments are directed at a better understanding of mechanism, and does not affect the author's primary argument for an intrinsic vs. extrinsic characterization. But I think might at the very least deserve some comment in a response or perhaps even a comment in the text.

One part of the MLE analysis I did not fully understand. The authors describe a procedure to reduce the data range (xmin, xmax) for the fitting. Why was this necessary? I would like to better understand the differences in fitting if this data pruning was not done. Perhaps one could gleam this information from the supplementary files, but looking it over it is not clear to me.

Reviewer #2:

In the foraging literature, Lévy walks (or truncated power laws) are of fundamental importance and are seen across the animal kingdom. Where do they come from? In this manuscript, Sims et al. propose that power law movement is generated intrinsically by the motion generating circuitry of Drosophila larvae. The fits certainly look like power laws and the authors provide evidence that larvae generate this even in the absence of a synaptic activity in the brain. Still, I have some concerns about the way the data is quantified and interpreted.

1) I would like to see some further quantification of how the analysis pipeline identifies turns. This is fundamental to the entirety of the manuscript but when I look at the examples of turns in Figure 4A I am not convinced that there are not large numbers of spurious turns. Are there thresholds that they can vary to ensure that this result isn't the effect of some spurious parameter?

2) I would also like some more insight into how path curvature relates to power law scaling of random walk step length. Many of these paths certainly look curved, and I know other worms such as C. elegans do have curved paths. Do Drosophila larvae? Is a curved path equivalent to a sequence of frequent turns?

3) Some quantification of turning angle seems like it would be useful as well. Can the authors clarify whether optimal search relies on uncorrelated turn angle? If you have a sequence of anticorrelated turns, you may get a power law alpha ~ 2.0 (for the sake of argument) but the animal would move outward in a ballistic fashion which is very different behaviorally. I am especially wondering about turns between short steps which are (I assume) very small and would look very different than the random walks you get in Viswanathan et al., 1999, or the authors' own Figure 1A, for instance.

4) Is there any adaptation to the turn rate, e.g. if you quantify exponent early vs. late is it the same? Many animals perform an area-restricted search when placed in a new environment, which might affect the overall measured exponent.

5) The authors perform a lot of manipulations to see if the animal will continue to produce Lévy flights and indeed they do (I am impressed they do anything with some of these manipulations). In fact, it seems impossible for them to do anything except Lévy flights. Have the authors considered a manipulation (puffing on odorants, for instance) that would induce a Brownian random walk and see if they revert to a Lévy flight or if they indeed continue on in a Lévy flight? Some of the manipulations, such as apoptosis experiment in the brain lobes in Figure 7D, suggest that the VNC (not CPGs per se) are what are driving the power law – but there could still be local sensory processing here. My concern here is that the authors may not be truly getting rid of the sensory processing that could drive the power law.

Reviewer #3:

This study is an excellent paper that should be published as soon as possible.

One of the most important open problems in theoretical ecology and movement ecology in particular is whether or not observed Lévy walk movement patterns (and similar behavior) are caused by intrinsic pattern generators implemented neurophysiologically. The other possibility is that such movement patterns are an emergent side-effect of how animals interact with the environment. The former explanation suggests that Lévy walks etc. are adaptive, whereas the latter explanation suggests that the behavior is not evolved. In this context, this paper gives what is close to a definitive answer to this longstanding question.

This is an experimental study that answers an important theoretical problem. claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claims.claim: There have been no studies to date that have unequivocally tested both the intrinsic and extrinsic hypotheses in the same model organism.
claims.source: Nevertheless, there have been no studies to date that have unequivocally tested both hypotheses in the same model organism.
claims.evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claims.claim: The ability to specifically and acutely manipulate neuronal activity in Drosophila larvae during a spatial exploration sequence makes it a suitable model for testing the Lévy foraging hypothesis.
claims.source: Our ability to specifically and acutely manipulate neuronal activity in Drosophila larvae during a spatial exploration sequence makes it a suitable model for testing the Lévy foraging hypothesis and to explore its mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a justification for the experimental approach based on the capabilities of the model system.

claims.claim: The turn angle distribution for all individual larva paths that were best fitted by truncated power-laws showed a near uniform distribution of large turn angles (50 and 175o, left or right).

claims.source: Analysis showed 11 (of 21 tracks) had best fits to truncated power-law distributions (Table 2; Supplementary file 3; Figure 5), with two tracks best fit by the exponential distribution and eight tracks best fit by neither distribution (Supplementary file 1).

Although this resulted in more exponential fits to step-length frequency distributions (10 tracks from 62 retained), it was striking that 37% of distributions were best fit by truncated power laws (Table 2; Supplementary file 1; Figure 7 and 8).

results.result: Control Drosophila larvae (BL/+, shits/+) with intact nervous systems exhibit Lévy-like movement patterns when tracked in environments with minimal external stimuli at both 22°C and 33°C. At 22°C, 70-79% of trajectories were best fit by truncated power-law distributions with mean exponents of 1.47-1.49, and at 33°C, 57-77% showed similar patterns. Multiple analyses (tortuosity, MSD, turn angle distributions) confirmed characteristics consistent with Lévy walks.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C64 provide converging evidence from multiple independent analytical approaches (MLE fitting, tortuosity analysis, MSD, turn angle distributions) all supporting Lévy-like patterns in control larvae. The quantitative results are internally consistent, include appropriate sample sizes (n=30-34), span multiple orders of magnitude (>1.5), and show robustness to methodological variations (C39-C42). The statistical analyses are rigorous and the conclusions are well-supported by the data.

results.result: BL>shits larvae with impaired brain and SOG function at 33°C exhibit Lévy-like movement patterns statistically indistinguishable from controls. Electrophysiology confirmed effective neural blockade (70-81% activity reduction), and 26 of 54 analyzable tracks were best fit by truncated power-laws with mean exponent 1.66±0.50, with 93% of the population predicted to fall within the Lévy range.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C72 demonstrate that Lévy-like patterns persist despite brain/SOG impairment, supported by both electrophysiological validation of the manipulation (C65) and multiple movement analyses (C68-C72). The lack of significant difference from controls (C71-C72) is appropriately interpreted, though the higher mean exponent (1.66 vs 1.35-1.54) warrants discussion. The convergence of evidence from independent measures strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Mushroom body activity does not significantly affect Lévy-like movement patterns in larvae. Both MB247/+ controls and MB247>shits larvae with blocked mushroom bodies showed 74% of tracks best fit by truncated power-laws, with mean exponents of 1.74 and 1.56 respectively that were not significantly different from controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 provide clear evidence that mushroom body function is not required for Lévy-like patterns. The similar proportions of power-law fits (74% in both conditions) and lack of significant difference in exponents (C77) support the conclusion. However, the study would benefit from reporting the statistical test used and effect sizes for the comparison.

results.result: BLsens>shits larvae with blocked brain, SOG, and all somatosensation exhibit Lévy-like patterns with mean exponent 1.96±0.39, remarkably close to the theoretical optimum of μ≅2.0. Of 21 analyzable tracks, 11 (52%) were best fit by truncated power-laws, with 81% of population exponents predicted to fall between 1.5-2.5.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 provide the strongest evidence for intrinsic generation of optimal Lévy patterns. The mean exponent of 1.96 is strikingly close to theoretical optimum (C83), and the CPD analysis (C84-C85) strengthens confidence in this result. However, the lower proportion of power-law fits (52% vs 70-79% in controls) and the observation that these larvae moved more slowly with fewer long steps (C80-C81) suggest the manipulation may have affected movement capacity, which could influence interpretation.

results.result: BLsens>rpr,hid larvae with induced apoptosis of brain and sensory neurons show Lévy-like patterns similar to UAS-shits experiments. At control temperature (22°C), 80% of tracks fit power-laws with exponent 1.51. At 32°C with induced apoptosis, 37% fit power-laws with mean exponent 2.14, significantly higher and closer to theoretical optimum than controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 provide independent validation using a different experimental approach (cell death vs. synaptic blockade). The convergence of results from two distinct methods (C90) strengthens confidence in the intrinsic hypothesis. However, the lower proportion of power-law fits at 32°C (37% vs 80% at 22°C) and more spatially restricted trajectories suggest the manipulation may have compromised movement capacity, requiring careful interpretation of the higher exponent (C88-C89).

results.result: The study provides strong evidence that Lévy-like movement patterns are generated intrinsically by the thoracic and abdominal nervous system, independent of brain, SOG, or sensory input. This represents the strongest evidence to date for intrinsic generation of Lévy-like patterns in animals, rejecting the extrinsic hypothesis that such patterns emerge from environmental interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 and C91-C99 synthesize the experimental findings into the main conclusion. The evidence is strong because: (1) multiple independent manipulations (BL>shits, BLsens>shits, BLsens>rpr,hid) all show Lévy-like patterns; (2) electrophysiology validates neural blockade; (3) exponents approach theoretical optimum (μ≅2.0); (4) patterns persist without brain/sensory function. However, the claim of 'strongest evidence' (C7, C92) is evaluative and depends on comparison to prior literature. The lower proportion of analyzable tracks and power-law fits in some manipulated conditions suggests some caveats.

results.result: The study employed rigorous data quality control and validated the robustness of analytical methods. Of 658 recorded tracks, 187 (28.4%) were excluded based on pre-defined criteria. Sensitivity analyses showed μ values were robust to variations in Kalman filter parameters and minimum resolution values, and movement patterns were stationary (no differences before/after collisions).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C42 describe methodological rigor and validation. The pre-defined exclusion criteria (C37-C38) are appropriate for Lévy walk analysis, and the sensitivity analyses (C39-C40) and stationarity tests (C41-C42) strengthen confidence in the results. The 28.4% exclusion rate is substantial but appears justified. These methodological validations are essential for supporting the main findings.

results.result: The restrictive temperature of 33°C did not affect feeding behavior or movement patterns in control larvae, as evidenced by no significant difference in power-law exponents between 22°C and 33°C for BL/+ or shits/+ larvae, indicating that movements at 33°C reflected normal searching behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 and C105 address an important control: whether the restrictive temperature itself affects behavior. The feeding assay (C46, Figure 3B) and lack of significant differences in exponents between temperatures (C105) support the interpretation that 33°C effects in manipulated larvae are due to neural blockade rather than temperature stress. This validation is critical for interpreting the main results.

results.result: The observed power-law exponents (μ=1.66 for BL>shits, μ=1.96 for BLsens>shits) are close to theoretically optimal values for Lévy searches. Theory predicts μ~2 is optimal across broad resource distributions, while μ~1.5 has lowest variance in foraging efficiency, suggesting Drosophila larval exploration patterns are similar to theoretically optimal Lévy searches for locating sparse and distant resources.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C104 connect experimental findings to theoretical predictions from the literature (C101-C103). The observed exponents fall within or near optimal ranges predicted by theory, strengthening the biological significance of the findings. However, the interpretation relies on theoretical work conducted in different contexts (simulations), and the actual resource distributions encountered by larvae in nature are unknown, which limits the strength of this functional interpretation.

results.result: The difference in exponents between control larvae (μ~1.35-1.54 at 33°C) and BL>shits larvae (μ=1.66) may result from sensory responses of controls to minimal external cues in the experimental setup, implying that the near-optimal search pattern of BL>shits larvae emerges from central pattern generation in the absence of external sensory inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 offer a speculative explanation for observed differences in exponents. While plausible, this interpretation is not directly tested and represents post-hoc reasoning. The claim that controls respond to 'minimal external cues' is not independently validated, and alternative explanations (e.g., effects of neural manipulation on movement mechanics) are not ruled out. This interpretation requires additional experimental support.

results.result: The study proposes a 'Lévy timing mechanism' (LTM) as a potential neural mechanism for generating Lévy-like patterns, whereby temporally scale-free changes in neuronal activity controlling transitions between crawls and turns could produce power-law distributed pause times. This mechanism could be analogous to 'fractal reorientation clocks' and related to scale-free neuronal avalanches observed in cortical networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C122 propose a mechanistic hypothesis but do not test it experimentally. The proposal draws on prior work about neural circuitry (C108-C110) and theoretical concepts (C111, C114-C120), but remains speculative (C112-C113). While the hypothesis is plausible and grounded in relevant literature, it requires direct experimental validation through measurements of pause time distributions and neural activity patterns during movement. The claim provides a framework for future work but is not supported by data in this study.

results.result: Multi-scale movement paths are generated intrinsically by the relatively simple thoracic and abdominal nervous system. The intrinsic Lévy-like patterns can be viewed as an underlying 'free running' optimal search pattern that is modulated by environmental stimuli when sensory inputs are received, with descending signals potentially switching from Lévy-like to deterministic movement patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C129 synthesize the findings into a conceptual model. The intrinsic generation by thoracic/abdominal circuits is well-supported by the experimental data (C123). The comparison to decerebrate vertebrates (C124-C127) provides useful context. However, the proposed modulation mechanism (C128-C129) is speculative and not directly tested in this study. The model is reasonable but the modulatory component requires experimental validation.

results.result: The fine-tuning of intrinsic movement patterns to theoretically optimal Lévy walks suggests selection pressure for these characteristics. Given that searching is crucial for survival and Lévy walks are optimal across diverse environments, the simple neural circuitry generating these patterns may have evolved early in nervous system evolution, potentially explaining the widespread occurrence of Lévy-like behavior across diverse taxa.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C134, C137, and C139 make evolutionary arguments based on the experimental findings and theoretical optimality. While the logic is reasonable—optimal search patterns should be under selection (C130-C132)—these claims are speculative. The study does not provide direct evidence for evolutionary adaptation, and alternative explanations (e.g., convergent evolution, acknowledged in C138) are not ruled out. The evolutionary claims extend beyond what the data can support and would require comparative studies across taxa and/or evolutionary modeling.

results.result: The introduction establishes the theoretical framework and controversy surrounding Lévy walks in animal movement. Lévy walks are theoretically optimal for blind foragers searching for sparse resources, have been observed across diverse taxa, but their origin (intrinsic vs. extrinsic) remains contentious with no unequivocal generative mechanism identified. Two competing hypotheses exist: intrinsic (endogenous neural processes) vs. extrinsic (emergent from environmental interactions).
